title: URI Design and Ownership
summary: This document explains how a URI scheme specification should treat the structure of URIs. It cautions that specs should not dictate the layout of paths and other parts of a site's URIs, because those belong to whoever owns the site. It was replaced by RFC 8820.

eli5.summary: A website owner picks the street names inside their own town. This RFC says outside rule-makers should not tell them what to call their streets. It was later replaced by a newer version.

questions: who owns the structure of a uri
can a standard mandate uri paths
subtitle: Standards should not dictate how a URI's owner structures their own URIs

tldr.problem: Specifications sometimes mandate that URIs must have specific structures, such as fixed paths or query parameters. This constrains the site owner's freedom and can cause collisions, interoperability problems, and operational difficulties.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines best practices for where specifications may constrain URI structure. Scheme definitions control overall structure; other specs may define well-known URIs for specific purposes but must not mandate arbitrary path layouts or query syntax.
tldr.outcome: Specifications should use URI templates, web linking (RFC 5988), or well-known URIs (RFC 5785) instead of constraining arbitrary URI structure. This preserves the owner's control and enables flexibility.

today: RFC 7320 is a Best Current Practice and remains in effect. It was replaced by RFC 8820, which consolidates and refines the guidance with additional examples and clearer language about when URIs can be constrained.

sections.title: URI Ownership and Control
sections.content: URIs often embed structured data, such as application information in the path, user data in the query, or application details in the authority. Many implementations and prepackaged applications have highly structured URIs that can only be changed in limited ways. However, the owner of the URI is responsible for choosing how to structure it. When a standard mandates particular URI structures, it usurps that ownership and can create several problems. Collisions occur when multiple ad hoc conventions become standardized and occupy the same URI space. Dilution happens when ephemeral information destabilizes the URI (see RFC 3986 Section 3.5.1). Rigidity occurs when fixed syntax prevents desired deployment patterns, such as running multiple applications on a single hostname when their mandatory paths conflict. Operational difficulties arise when a standard requires a URI structure that specific implementations cannot support, such as specifying query parameters for systems that only serve static filesystem files. Client assumptions cause interoperability breakage: clients may assume that any URI matching a standardized convention conforms to that standard, leading to false positives.
sections.eli5: If someone invents a rule that the 'sig' query parameter always means a cryptographic signature, and a website already uses 'sig' for something else, now they collide and confuse everyone.

sections.title: Best Practices for Each URI Component
sections.content: URI schemes define the presence, format and semantics of all URI components. Other specifications MUST update the scheme definition itself to mandate substructure; updating RFC 3986 is an exceptional circumstance reserved for BCP 115. For URI authorities, all specifications besides the scheme MUST NOT constrain the structure or semantics unless they update the scheme; applications MAY nominate the port they use if properly registered. For URI paths, scheme definitions control what is allowed; all other specifications MUST NOT constrain path structure, with one exception: RFC 5785 well-known URIs allow registrations for specific purposes like '.well-known/acme-challenge' for ACME certificate validation. For queries, the presence and format depend on many factors and the implementation; applications MUST NOT directly specify query syntax, and extensions MUST NOT constrain query semantics. For fragment identifiers, media type definitions SHOULD specify fragment syntax; other specifications MUST NOT define fragment structure unless explicitly creating one for reuse by media types.
sections.eli5: The URL scheme (http, https) decides the big picture. After that, the website owner decides everything: paths, query parameters, all of it. A standard can only jump in if it's updating the scheme itself, which almost never happens.

sections.title: Better Strategies Than Fixed URI Structures
sections.content: Instead of mandating URI structure, specifications should use mechanisms designed to preserve owner control. RFC 5988 specifies relation types for web links, allowing applications to define link semantics and connectivity without constraining paths or queries. RFC 6570 provides URI Templates, a standard syntax for dynamically inserting application variables into URIs, enabling flexibility while avoiding fixed structures. RFC 5785 reserves specific well-known paths for standard use on 'http' and 'https' URIs when the scheme opts in; this is not a general escape valve but a targeted mechanism for discovery points. Simply prefixing query parameters with a namespace like 'myapp_' does not solve the problem because the prefix itself is subject to collision risk. More elaborate structures to avoid collisions are not acceptable solutions and do not address the core issues.
sections.eli5: Instead of saying 'you must have /myapp', send links that say 'go here' without assuming the path. Or use templates where the path can change. Or register a special well-known path if you really need a standard spot to discover something.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content: This RFC does not introduce new protocol artifacts with security considerations. It prohibits practices that might introduce vulnerabilities. If a security-sensitive mechanism assumes a particular URI path or query parameter has special meaning, false positives can occur when other sites already use the same structure for unrelated purposes. For example, if a specification requires that any query parameter named 'token' is a bearer token, then any existing parameter with that name on any site could be misinterpreted as a bearer token, compromising security. Constraining URI structure can also create situations where implementations guess at meanings that are not intended. Allowing sites to own their URI space prevents these assumptions from breaking interoperability. Site owners should also ensure that URI structure itself is not used as a security mechanism, as URIs are often recorded in logs and headers visible to intermediaries.
sections.eli5: If a standard assumes every 'token' query parameter is a secret code, a website that uses 'token' for something harmless could accidentally leak it. Let each site control their own names, and you avoid these false alarms.
